etymology: English Puritan pastor (1616-1679), vicar of Lavenham in Suffolk, author of The Christian in Complete Armour.
biblical_def: William Gurnall was an English Puritan minister, vicar of Lavenham in Suffolk, remembered above all for one massive and enduring work: The Christian in Complete Armour, a vast practical exposition of the Christian's spiritual warfare from Ephesians 6:10-20. For more than a thousand pages Gurnall unfolds the whole armor of God piece by piece — the girdle of truth, the breastplate of righteousness, the shield of faith, the helmet of salvation, the sword of the Spirit — pressing each upon the conscience with searching application and vivid imagery. Spurgeon said the book was "peerless and priceless," and that every line was full of wisdom. Gurnall's theme is that the Christian life is unrelenting combat against sin, Satan, and the world, and that the believer must be armed wholly in Christ, for partial armor is no armor at all. He conformed at the Restoration and kept his living, which brought him criticism from some nonconformists, yet his book has fed warring saints of every party ever since. Gurnall stands in the dictionary as the great Puritan anatomist of spiritual warfare, who taught the church that grace does not exempt the believer from battle but equips him for it.
webster_summary: English Puritan pastor (1616-1679) of Lavenham, author of The Christian in Complete Armour, the great Puritan exposition of the believer's spiritual warfare from Ephesians 6; prized by Spurgeon as peerless and priceless.

corruption_summary: Gurnall's legacy is corrupted when the Puritans are caricatured as joyless legalists, and when the New Testament's call to spiritual warfare is softened into a comfortable religion with no enemy and no battle.
corruption_paragraphs: Killjoy-caricature correction. The popular slander paints the Puritans as dour, repressive, and joyless. Gurnall's life and book refute it: here is a pastor of vivid imagination, warm pastoral tenderness, and bracing hope, who armed weary saints for the fight with a thousand pages of comfort and counsel. The dictionary holds that the Puritan vision of the Christian life — serious, joyful, and full-blooded — is a treasure to recover, not a stereotype to repeat.

Warfare-denied misreading. Modern religion often empties the faith of conflict, offering self-improvement without an enemy. Gurnall recalls the church to the New Testament's sober realism: we wrestle against principalities and powers, and the believer who is not armed is already losing. The dictionary recovers the doctrine of spiritual warfare — the world, the flesh, and the devil are real foes, and the whole armor of God, which is Christ Himself, is the only sufficient defense.

etymology: English Puritan preacher (1599-1646), Congregationalist, member of the Westminster Assembly, author of The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment.
biblical_def: Jeremiah Burroughs was an English Puritan preacher and a member of the Westminster Assembly, best known for his classic treatise The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment, an exposition of Paul's words, "I have learned, in whatsoever state I am, therewith to be content" (Phil 4:11). Burroughs defines Christian contentment as "that sweet, inward, quiet, gracious frame of spirit, which freely submits to and delights in God's wise and fatherly disposal in every condition." He distinguishes it sharply from stoic indifference and worldly resignation: it is not the absence of feeling but the presence of grace, a learned and supernatural calm that flows from trust in the sovereignty and goodness of God. Burroughs was famously irenic in a contentious age, laboring for peace among the godly; the motto often linked to him reads, "in necessary things, unity; in doubtful things, liberty; in all things, charity." His other works include Gospel Worship and The Evil of Evils, on the sinfulness of sin. Burroughs stands in the dictionary as the great Puritan teacher of contentment — not as passive fatalism, but as the soul's restful submission to and delight in the providence of a wise and fatherly God.
webster_summary: English Puritan preacher (1599-1646) and Westminster divine, author of The Rare Jewel of Christian Contentment on Philippians 4:11; teacher of contentment as the soul's restful delight in God's fatherly providence, and a famously irenic peacemaker.

corruption_summary: Burroughs's teaching is corrupted when contentment is confused with stoic apathy or prosperity-driven striving, or when the Puritans are caricatured as gloomy when in fact they prized a deep and settled joy.
corruption_paragraphs: Stoicism-confused misreading. Some mistake Christian contentment for the Stoic's suppression of feeling or the fatalist's grim resignation. Burroughs labors to distinguish them: true contentment is not numbness but a gracious, supernatural restfulness that submits to and delights in God's fatherly will. The dictionary holds the difference — the believer is not steeled against providence but melted by trust in the God who orders it, content because the hand that disposes is a Father's.

Joyless-Puritan caricature. The modern myth of the gloomy Puritan collapses before Burroughs, who called contentment a "rare jewel" and made the pursuit of settled joy in God his life's theme. The dictionary recovers the truth that the Puritans were physicians of the soul who prescribed deep and durable gladness in God, against both the discontent of the flesh and the false cheer of the world.

etymology: English nonconformist minister (1662-1714), son of Philip Henry, author of the Exposition of the Old and New Testaments (Matthew Henry's Commentary).
biblical_def: Matthew Henry was an English nonconformist minister, the son of the ejected Puritan Philip Henry, and the author of the most beloved devotional commentary in the English language, his Exposition of the Old and New Testaments. For decades a pastor at Chester and later at Hackney, Henry poured his life into expounding the whole Bible verse by verse with a rare blend of doctrinal soundness, practical wisdom, and warm, memorable application. He completed the work through the book of Acts before his death; godly ministers finished the Epistles and Revelation from his notes. His comments are famous for their quotable turns of phrase and their relentless pressing of the text upon heart and life — Whitefield read the whole commentary four times, twice on his knees, and Spurgeon urged every minister to read it through. Henry's aim was never mere information but transformation: he handles every passage to feed faith, rebuke sin, comfort the afflicted, and exalt Christ. He stands in the dictionary as the great popular expositor of Scripture, who made the riches of Puritan exegesis accessible to ordinary believers and taught generations to read the Bible for the nourishment of the soul.
webster_summary: English nonconformist minister (1662-1714), author of the Exposition of the Old and New Testaments, the most beloved devotional commentary in English; prized by Whitefield and Spurgeon for its blend of doctrine, wisdom, and warm application.

corruption_summary: Henry's legacy is honored by recovering the practice of devotional, Christ-centered Bible exposition for ordinary believers, against both cold academic criticism and the modern neglect of patient meditation on the whole Word.
corruption_paragraphs: Criticism-over-devotion misreading. Modern biblical studies have often prized critical dissection over devotional nourishment, treating the text as an object to analyze rather than a word to obey. Henry models the older and better way: rigorous attention to the sense of Scripture married to relentless application to the soul. The dictionary holds that the end of exposition is not information but the feeding of faith and the exalting of Christ, and commends Henry's method as a corrective to a merely academic handling of the Word.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is meditation on the whole counsel of God. Henry expounded every book and every chapter, refusing to neglect any part of Scripture, and pressed each upon the conscience. In an age of fragmentary, topical reading, the dictionary recovers his example of patient, comprehensive, prayerful engagement with the entire Bible as the daily bread of the believing soul.

etymology: English Puritan theologian (1624-1679), author of the Latin Synopsis Criticorum and the English Annotations upon the Holy Bible.
biblical_def: Matthew Poole was an English Puritan theologian and biblical scholar, renowned for two monumental works of exposition. The first, his Synopsis Criticorum Biblicorum, was a vast Latin digest gathering and weighing the comments of scores of interpreters on every verse of Scripture — a labor of ten years that distilled the learning of the church into one critical apparatus for ministers. The second, his English Annotations upon the Holy Bible, brought sound, concise exposition within reach of ordinary readers; Poole completed it through Isaiah 58 before his death, and other Puritan divines finished it from his plan. Poole was a man of method and clarity, valued for sober judgment rather than flights of rhetoric, and he wrote in defense of Protestant truth against Rome. Forced to flee during the anti-Protestant frenzy of the so-called Popish Plot, he died in exile at Amsterdam. He stands in the dictionary as the great Puritan harmonizer of interpreters, who served the church by gathering, sifting, and clarifying the best of biblical scholarship, that pastor and people alike might understand the Scriptures rightly and hold fast the faith once delivered.
webster_summary: English Puritan biblical scholar (1624-1679), author of the Latin Synopsis Criticorum and the English Annotations upon the Holy Bible; the great Puritan harmonizer of interpreters, valued for sober judgment and clear exposition.

corruption_summary: Poole's example honors the recovery of careful, comparative, reverent biblical scholarship in the service of the church, against both lazy interpretation and a criticism that doubts rather than illumines the text.
corruption_paragraphs: Doubt-driven criticism misreading. Much modern scholarship turns its learning against the Scriptures, using the comparison of sources to undermine confidence in the Word. Poole turned the same comparative labor to the opposite end: gathering interpreters to illumine the text and confirm the faith. The dictionary holds that true scholarship serves the authority of Scripture; the sifting of many voices should clarify the meaning God intended, not dissolve it into a fog of uncertainty.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is reverent diligence in study. Poole gave a decade to weighing the comments of others verse by verse, that the church might understand rightly. The dictionary commends his example to a hurried age: the Word of God rewards patient, careful, comparative study, and the minister is called to be a workman who rightly divides the word of truth (2 Tim 2:15).

etymology: English Puritan minister (1630-1705), domestic chaplain to Oliver Cromwell, author of The Living Temple and The Blessedness of the Righteous.
biblical_def: John Howe was an English Puritan minister of unusual breadth and elevation of mind, who served for a time as domestic chaplain to Oliver Cromwell and, after the Restoration and his ejection, ministered among the nonconformists with a notably catholic and peaceable spirit. His most famous work, The Living Temple, argues from the nature of God and man that the human soul was made to be the dwelling-place of God, ruined by sin yet destined to be restored as God's temple through redemption. Other works, such as The Blessedness of the Righteous and On Delighting in God, breathe the same air of lofty, reverent meditation on the greatness and goodness of God and the soul's chief end in communion with Him. Howe combined deep learning with a warm, contemplative piety, and labored for unity among the godly across party lines without surrendering the substance of the Reformed faith. He stands in the dictionary as the Puritan of magnanimous spirit and elevated devotion, who taught the church that man was made for God, that sin has unhoused the divine Guest, and that grace rebuilds the soul into a living temple for the glory of its Maker.
webster_summary: English Puritan minister (1630-1705), chaplain to Cromwell, author of The Living Temple; a man of broad learning, catholic spirit, and elevated devotion who taught that the soul was made to be the dwelling-place of God.

corruption_summary: Howe's vision is honored by recovering the truth that man was made for communion with God as His temple, against a secular anthropology that reduces the human person to matter, appetite, or self-definition.
corruption_paragraphs: Reductive-anthropology misreading. The modern world defines man as a clever animal, a bundle of needs, or a self-made identity, with no Maker and no end beyond himself. Howe's Living Temple answers from the nature of things: man was framed to house the presence of God, and only in that indwelling communion is he whole. The dictionary holds the high biblical doctrine of man — made in God's image for God's fellowship, ruined by sin, restored in Christ — against every account that empties the human person of its God-ward purpose.

This entry faces little direct postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the soul's chief end. Howe's lofty devotion fixed on the greatness and goodness of God as the one worthy object of the heart. In an age of distraction and self-absorption, the dictionary commends his example of elevated, God-centered meditation, and his conviction that the restless human soul finds rest only when God again dwells within His temple.

etymology: English-born bishop and Puritan writer (1634-1690), Bishop of Derry in Ireland, author of expositions of the Ten Commandments and the Lord's Prayer.
biblical_def: Ezekiel Hopkins was an English-born preacher and bishop, eventually Bishop of Derry in Ireland, whose doctrinal sympathies were thoroughly Puritan and whose practical writings have outlived his episcopal office. His most enduring work is a full and searching Exposition of the Ten Commandments, which anatomizes the moral law with great spiritual penetration, showing the breadth of each commandment, the sins it forbids, and the duties it requires, and driving the convicted sinner to Christ. He wrote likewise on the Lord's Prayer, on the two covenants, on regeneration, and on the vanity of the world and glory of Christ. Hopkins held the law in the classic Reformed manner: it cannot justify, for no man keeps it, yet it remains the perfect rule of righteousness, exposing sin, restraining evil, and guiding the believer in the way of obedience. He stands in the dictionary as a master expositor of the moral law, who taught the church that the Ten Commandments are not abolished by grace but established by it, serving as a schoolmaster to bring sinners to Christ and a lamp to light the believer's grateful obedience.
webster_summary: English-born bishop and Puritan writer (1634-1690), Bishop of Derry, author of a searching Exposition of the Ten Commandments; a master expositor of the moral law in the classic Reformed manner.

corruption_summary: Hopkins's work guards against antinomianism, which discards the moral law altogether, and against legalism, which abuses it for justification; both errors miss the law's true Reformed uses.
corruption_paragraphs: Antinomian misreading. A common modern error treats the Ten Commandments as obsolete under grace, as though the gospel freed believers from the moral law itself. Hopkins, with the whole Reformed tradition, holds the opposite: Christ came not to destroy the law but to fulfil it, and the believer, justified by faith, delights in the law as the rule of grateful obedience. The dictionary recovers the law's abiding place — it cannot save, but it is holy, just, and good, and grace writes it on the heart.

Legalist misreading. The opposite error abuses the law for self-justification, imagining that commandment-keeping earns God's favor. Hopkins exposes this too: the law's first work is to convict, to strip the sinner of self-righteousness and drive him to Christ as the schoolmaster drives the pupil. The dictionary holds the classic three uses of the law — to restrain, to convict, and to guide — against both the antinomian who discards it and the legalist who misuses it.

etymology: English Puritan minister (1634-1678), ejected in 1662, author of an influential explication of the Westminster Shorter Catechism.
biblical_def: Thomas Vincent was an English Puritan minister, ejected from the Church of England in the Great Ejection of 1662, who labored on through plague and persecution as a faithful pastor of nonconformist congregations in London. He is best remembered for An Explication of the Assembly's Shorter Catechism, a clear and warm exposition that opens each question and answer of the Westminster Shorter Catechism with proof, application, and supporting Scripture — long a standard help for teaching the faith to young and old. During the Great Plague of 1665, when many ministers fled, Vincent stayed to preach to the dying and bury the dead, and recorded those terrible days in God's Terrible Voice in the City, on the plague and the Fire of London as the chastening calls of God. He also wrote Christ's Sudden and Certain Appearance to Judgment, pressing the reality of the last day upon the conscience. Vincent stands in the dictionary as a model catechist and faithful plague-time pastor, who taught the church that sound doctrine must be learned, understood, and applied, and that the minister's place is beside his people in the hour of death, pointing them to Christ and the judgment to come.

corruption_paragraphs: Catechesis-neglected correction. The modern church often abandons the patient teaching of doctrine for entertainment and vague feeling. Vincent's life rebukes the trend: he gave himself to opening the catechism question by question, that believers might know what they believe and why. The dictionary holds that catechesis is not a relic but a duty — the deliberate handing on of sound words to children and converts — and commends Vincent's explication as a model of teaching the faith with clarity and warmth.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is pastoral courage before death. When plague emptied London and many fled, Vincent stayed to preach to the dying and bury the dead. The dictionary commends his example: the shepherd's place is with the flock in the valley of the shadow, pointing the perishing to Christ and bidding them, in God's terrible voice, prepare to meet their God.

etymology: Welsh Puritan preacher (1618-1651), Presbyterian, beheaded under the Commonwealth; author of sermons on heaven, hell, and the soul.
biblical_def: Christopher Love was a Welsh-born Puritan preacher of fervent and affecting power, a convinced Presbyterian who ministered in London during the upheavals of the English Civil War and the Commonwealth. Converted as a youth under the preaching of William Erbery, he became a bold and popular preacher, much used to awaken sinners and comfort saints. His sermons, gathered after his death into volumes such as The Penitent Pardoned and treatises on heaven and hell and the soul's immortality, press eternal realities upon the conscience with great earnestness. Love's life ended in martyrdom of a kind: a firm Presbyterian opposed to the execution of the king and to the Independent ascendancy, he was implicated in a plot to restore the monarchy and was beheaded on Tower Hill in 1651, dying with notable composure and faith, his wife's tender letters to him in prison surviving as a memorial of godly affection under the shadow of death. Love stands in the dictionary as a fervent Puritan preacher and a martyr of conscience, who proclaimed heaven and hell with burning seriousness and met his own death in the sure hope of the glory he had preached.
webster_summary: Welsh Puritan preacher (1618-1651), a fervent Presbyterian beheaded under the Commonwealth; a powerful preacher of heaven, hell, and the soul who met his own death with composure and faith.

And as it is appointed unto men once to die, but after this the judgment:
corruption_summary: Love's preaching honors the recovery of heaven and hell as urgent realities, against a sentimental religion that has muted eternity, and his death honors the costliness of conscience against expediency.
corruption_paragraphs: Eternity-muted correction. Much modern preaching has fallen silent about heaven and hell, trading eternal realities for present therapeutic comfort. Love preached them with burning seriousness, pressing upon his hearers the weight of the soul's everlasting destiny. The dictionary holds that the certainty of death and judgment, the reality of heaven and hell, belong to the church's faithful proclamation; to mute them is to flatter sinners on the road to ruin and to rob saints of their hope.

This entry faces little postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the costliness of conscience. Love would not bend his Presbyterian convictions to the prevailing power, and it cost him his head. The dictionary commends, with sober discernment of his turbulent age, the example of a man who held his convictions under the shadow of the scaffold and met death in the hope of the glory he had preached, faithful unto death for the crown of life.
roots_summary: Welsh Puritan preacher (1618-1651), a fervent Presbyterian beheaded under the Commonwealth; a powerful preacher of heaven, hell, and the soul.

etymology: English Puritan minister (1628-1680), author of The Gospel Mystery of Sanctification.
biblical_def: Walter Marshall was an English Puritan minister remembered for a single, profound book that has shaped Reformed teaching on holiness ever since: The Gospel Mystery of Sanctification. Marshall's great theme is that sanctification, like justification, is received by faith and flows from union with Christ — not by the sinner's anxious self-reformation under the law, but by believing reception of the new nature, the Spirit, and the very righteousness of Christ. He had himself labored long under a heavy, defeated conscience, striving to mend his life by effort and finding no peace, until he came to see that the power to obey is itself a gift of grace, laid up in Christ and received by faith. The believer is first united to Christ and endowed with His Spirit, and from that union holiness grows as fruit from a living branch. Marshall thus guards holiness from two errors at once: the legalism that tries to be holy in order to be accepted, and the antinomianism that thinks acceptance makes holiness optional. He stands in the dictionary as the great Puritan physician of sanctification, who taught the church that we are made holy the same way we are justified — by faith in Christ, from whom both pardon and power flow.
webster_summary: English Puritan minister (1628-1680), author of The Gospel Mystery of Sanctification; taught that holiness, like justification, is received by faith from union with Christ, guarding against both legalism and antinomianism.
webster_full: WALTER MARSHALL, proper noun. English Puritan minister (1628-1680).

Taught that sanctification is received by faith from union with Christ.
Came to peace after long bondage under a defeated, law-driven conscience.
Guarded holiness from both legalism and antinomianism.
scriptures: John 15:5
I am the vine, ye are the branches: He that abideth in me, and I in him, the same bringeth forth much fruit: for without me ye can do nothing.
Gal 2:20

I am crucified with Christ: nevertheless I live; yet not I, but Christ liveth in me: and the life which I now live in the flesh I live by the faith of the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself for me.
Phil 2:13
For it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure.
But of him are ye in Christ Jesus, who of God is made unto us wisdom, and righteousness, and sanctification, and redemption:
corruption_summary: Marshall's teaching corrects two perennial errors: the legalism that pursues holiness to earn acceptance, and the antinomianism that treats holiness as optional once accepted; both sever sanctification from union with Christ.
corruption_paragraphs: Legalist misreading. The anxious soul tries to become holy by sheer effort under the law, hoping thereby to win God's favor, and finds only defeat — the very bondage Marshall himself long endured. He learned that the power to obey is a gift received by faith from Christ, not a wage earned by striving. The dictionary holds with Marshall that we do not work for acceptance but from it; holiness is the fruit of union with Christ, not the price of it.

Antinomian misreading. The opposite error concludes that, since holiness does not earn acceptance, it may be neglected. Marshall closes this door as firmly as the other: the same faith that receives Christ for justification receives Him for sanctification, and union with the living Vine necessarily bears fruit. The dictionary recovers the balance — justification and sanctification are distinct gifts, never separated, both flowing by faith from the one Christ in whom the believer is made righteous and holy.

etymology: English Puritan theologian (d. 1664), member of the Westminster Assembly, author of Spiritual Refining and Vindiciae Legis.
biblical_def: Anthony Burgess was an English Puritan theologian and a member of the Westminster Assembly, a learned and prolific defender of Reformed orthodoxy against the errors of his day. His major works include Spiritual Refining, a vast treatise on the doctrine of assurance and on indwelling sin and hypocrisy, searching the heart to distinguish true grace from its counterfeits; Vindiciae Legis, a defense of the moral law against the antinomians who would cast it off; and a full treatment of justification. Burgess wrote at a time when the gospel of free grace was being abused by some into lawlessness, and he labored to hold both truths together: that the believer is justified freely by faith apart from works, and that the moral law remains the believer's rule of grateful obedience. In Spiritual Refining he gives some of the most careful Puritan analysis of assurance ever written, teaching that genuine faith may be tested and known by its fruits, yet that assurance is God's gift and not the ground of acceptance. Burgess stands in the dictionary as a Westminster divine and a master of the doctrine of assurance, who defended the law against antinomianism and taught the church to discern true saving grace from its many imitations.
webster_summary: English Puritan theologian (d. 1664) and Westminster divine, author of Spiritual Refining (on assurance and indwelling sin) and Vindiciae Legis (defending the moral law against antinomianism).

scriptures: Examine yourselves, whether ye be in the faith; prove your own selves. Know ye not your own selves, how that Jesus Christ is in you, except ye be reprobates?
Wherefore the rather, brethren, give diligence to make your calling and election sure: for if ye do these things, ye shall never fall:

corruption_summary: Burgess's work corrects antinomianism, which casts off the moral law, and false assurance, which presumes grace without examining the heart; both pervert the gospel of free grace.
corruption_paragraphs: Antinomian misreading. In Burgess's day, as in ours, some turned the doctrine of free grace into a license to neglect the law, claiming that faith makes obedience irrelevant. His Vindiciae Legis answers that faith establishes the law rather than voiding it (Rom 3:31): the believer is freed from the law as a covenant of works, but the moral law remains his rule of grateful obedience. The dictionary holds this balance against every lawless distortion of grace.

False-assurance misreading. The opposite peril is a presumptuous confidence that claims salvation without any evidence of grace. Burgess's Spiritual Refining teaches the church to examine itself (2 Cor 13:5), distinguishing true faith from hypocrisy by its fruits, while grounding assurance not in works but in Christ. The dictionary recovers his careful path between presumption and despair: assurance is a gift to be sought and tested, never a substitute for the self-examination Scripture commands.
